name: Mexico City Metropolitan Cathedral

hotspots.name: West bell tower
hotspots.details: The two square bell towers were designed by José Damián Ortiz de Castro in the late 18th century. They have earthquake-conscious upper stages and are capped with bell-shaped roofs of tezontle finished in chiluca stone, each roof ending in a sphere and a cross.

hotspots.name: East bell tower
hotspots.details: Together the towers can hold many bells; the Mexico City government notes that the belfries can house as many as 56, with 35 in place today. In 2008 a time capsule from 1791 was taken from the top of the east tower and replaced with a new one.

hotspots.name: Clock and theological virtues
hotspots.details: Manuel Tolsá finished the exterior in 1813. He added the neoclassical clock structure at the top of the main façade and crowned it with sculptures of Faith, Hope and Charity, the three theological virtues.

hotspots.name: Main south façade
hotspots.details: The cathedral faces south onto the Zócalo. Its principal façade brings together styles from the long building campaign: Renaissance, Baroque and Neoclassical. Three portals open in this front.

hotspots.name: Central portal
hotspots.details: The marble relief above the central door shows the Assumption of Mary, the dedication of the cathedral (Catedral Metropolitana de la Asunción de la Santísima Virgen María a los Cielos). The side doors show Saint Peter receiving the keys and the ship of the Church.

hotspots.name: Side portal
hotspots.details: Beside the main door, the façade has two flanking portals. The cathedral as a whole has four façades with columned, statued doorways; this south front is the ceremonial face toward the plaza.

hotspots.name: Dome and lantern
hotspots.details: Tolsá rebuilt the crossing dome, which had been low and squat. He opened a wider ring and raised a taller lantern so the dome would sit in better proportion above the transept.

hotspots.name: Nave
hotspots.details: Claudio de Arciniega laid out the plan in the 16th century. Seven naves were first proposed; they were reduced to five. Inside, those naves run to a crossing under the dome, with a choir and two large 18th-century organs in the central vessel.

hotspots.name: Apse (north end)
hotspots.details: Because the church faces south, the liturgical head of the building is at the north. There the Capilla de los Reyes (Chapel of the Kings) holds Jerónimo de Balbás's Altar of the Kings, and the archbishops' crypt lies below.

hotspots.name: Sagrario Metropolitano
hotspots.details: The parish tabernacle attached to the cathedral's east side is a masterwork of Mexican Baroque. It was built between 1749 and 1768 to designs by Lorenzo Rodríguez, with façades that mix pale chiluca stone and red tezontle in estipite pilasters and niches of apostles.

hotspots.name: Buttresses
hotspots.details: Heavy stone buttresses line the long flanks and help carry the vaults of the five-nave interior (51 vaults, 74 arches and 40 columns in the usual description of the building). The cathedral stands on the soft lake-bed of old Tenochtitlan and has long needed structural care because of uneven settling.

hotspots.name: Roof balustrade
hotspots.details: When Tolsá completed the exterior he tied the long roofline together with cornices and balustrades, adding decorative urns along the parapet. Those rails run above the nave and around the clock stage on the main façade.
